title: Greenhouse Gas Inventory FY 2025
text: 1 Summary

title: Greenhouse Gas Inventory FY 2025
text:
1.1 Background
The Town of Amherst Massachusetts seeks to achieve net zero community emissions by 2050, an ambitious goal set by the Town’s Energy and Climate Action Committee (ECAC) in their 2021 Climate Action, Adaptation, and Resilience Plan (CAARP). Using the 2016 emissions inventory as a baseline, the intermediary goals of 25% reduction in emissions by 2025 and 50% reduction in emissions by 2030 were set as well.
To accurately assess progress toward the ultimate goal of carbon neutrality, periodic emissions inventories are essential for tracking emissions trends and evaluating the effectiveness of climate action initiatives. This report seeks to determine whether the Town has achieved their 2025 target, to evaluate progress toward future milestones, to identify areas of success, and to identify areas that require further intervention.

title: Greenhouse Gas Inventory FY 2025
text:
1.2 Progress So Far
The Town has made significant progress toward achieving its 2025 emissions reduction target. There are numbers that exist to support this, but I have not finalized them, so this paragraph is really just a placeholder so I can get a sense of how things look before I get the aforementioned numbers.

title: 2  Municipal Overview
text:
2.1 Progress to Date
The Town of Amherst Municipality was responsible for 4487.6 Metric Tons of CO2 Equivalent emissions in FY 2016. In FY 2025, this number was 3,732. This represents a 16.8% decrease in municipal emissions relative to the 2016 baseline, which failed to meet the Town’s 25% emissions reduction goal for 2025. To meet the 2030 goal, the Town would need to reach 2,244 MTCO2e emissions, which represents a near 40% decrease in current emissions over the span of 5 years.

title: 2  Municipal Overview
text:
2.2 Emissions by Sector
Municipal emissions fall into two categories: stationary energy and transportation. Stationary energy accounted for 73.9% of total emissions in 2025, up from 68.6% in 2022. As it has been reported, electricity usage from electric vehicles (EVs) has been absorbed into stationary energy, so this increase in electricity consumption may reflect the increased adoption of EVs and their miscategorization as stationary energy, rather than a simple reduction in transportation emissions.

This is consistent with the Town’s move toward more renewable energy sources.

3.1.2 Emissions by Facility Category
Buildings are responsible for the largest share of municipal emissions, accounting for 59.5% of stationary emissions for FY 2025. The next largest share is accounted for by water and sewer facilities, which amounts to 36.6% in FY 2025. The remaining emissions are attributed to open spaces and street/traffic lights, which account for the remaining 3.9%.

3.2 Electricity
Electricity consumption increased significantly from 5674 megawatt hours (MWh) in FY 2022 to 6242 MWh in FY 2025, though this still represents a decrease from the FY 2016 consumption of 6398 MWh. Electricity consumption has increased steadily since the sharp decline in FY 2020 and FY 2021 due to the COVID-19 pandemic, and current levels in FY 2025 are much more typical of pre-pandemic usage.

title: 5  Municipal Key Findings
text: 5.1 Key Findings

title: 5  Municipal Key Findings
text:
Municipal emissions fell by 16.8% from FY 2016 to FY 2025, falling short of the 25% reduction target outlined in the CAARP.
Stationary energy emissions fell 15.4% between FY 2016 and FY 2025, though they have slightly increased by 78 MTCO2e since FY 2022.
Buildings accounted for approximately 60% of all municipal emissions in FY 2025.
Elementary schools were responsible for 795.5 MTCO2e emissions in 2025. Once the new, more energy efficient, elementary school is in use, the reduction in emissions could meaningfully change the trajectory of municipal emissions as a whole.
Transportation related municipal emissions dropped by 22.3% between FY 2016 and FY 2025.
The Fire Department is the only major fleet group (others groups include Police Department, Public Works, and School) that has increased their emissions since 2016, all others reduced emissions.

title: 5  Municipal Key Findings
text:
5.2 Municipal Emissions in Context
While it is important to analyze and address municipal emissions, as this is what the Town has direct control over, it is also important to understand the Town’s place in the context of broader community emissions. Municipal emissions only account for about 3.13% of total community emissions. Since the Town directly controls only a small fraction of emissions, achieving community-wide emissions goals requires action by residents, institutions, businesses, and higher education partners in addition to municipal action.
